ifsca-cmi.title: IFSCA (Capital Market Intermediaries) Regulations, 2025
ifsca-cmi.description: In-depth guide covering regulatory approvals, net worth thresholds, governance, client onboarding, and statutory returns for GIFT City intermediaries.

lessons.title: Why registration is the whole ballgame

payload.hook: Before a single trade, rating, or advice note, one question decides whether you exist in GIFT-IFSC at all: are you registered as a Capital Market Intermediary? Get the gate wrong and everything downstream is unauthorised. This module is that gate.

cards.title: Eleven activities, one certificate each
cards.law: A unit in IFSC desirous of undertaking any of the listed activities shall obtain a certificate of registration from the Authority (Reg 4(1)).
cards.means: If your activity is on the Reg 4 list, you cannot operate without an IFSCA certificate. If it is not on the list, these regulations do not gate it.
cards.watch: The list is exhaustive. Don't assume a hybrid service is exempt — map it to the nearest listed activity first.
cards.link: Sets up every category playbook in Part 2.

cards.title: Unified registration (since 12 Jan 2026)
cards.law: Proviso to Reg 4(1): a unit undertaking multiple activities may obtain a unified registration, in such manner as may be specified.
cards.means: A multi-desk unit can now hold one unified registration instead of collecting a separate certificate per activity.
cards.watch: Unified registration is NOT unified compliance — each activity still carries its own Chapter IV obligations and its own Part B conduct code.
cards.link: This is the seed of the 'common-or-entity' theme.

cards.title: Company/LLP/body corporate/branch — perpetual
cards.law: Reg 6: a CMI must be present in IFSC as a company, LLP, body corporate, or branch thereof. Reg 13: the certificate is perpetual unless suspended or cancelled.
cards.means: You need a recognised legal vehicle in the IFSC, and once granted, registration does not lapse on a renewal cycle.
cards.watch: 'Perpetual' surprises those used to periodic renewals elsewhere — there is no validity expiry to diarise, only suspension/cancellation risk.
cards.link: Contrast with SEBI-style periodic renewals.

payload.summary: Reg 4 lists eleven registrable activities, each needing an IFSCA certificate; since 12 Jan 2026 a multi-activity unit may hold one unified registration; the vehicle must be a company/LLP/body corporate/branch (Reg 6); and the certificate is perpetual unless suspended or cancelled (Reg 13).
payload.tip: Build an activity-to-obligation matrix on day one: list each activity the unit performs, the certificate that covers it, and the Chapter IV + Part B obligations it drags along. Unified registration makes this matrix more important, not less.

lessons.title: Obligation to seek Registration

payload.reg_text: A unit in IFSC desirous of undertaking any of the below mentioned activities shall obtain a certificate of registration from the Authority: (a) Broker dealer; (b) Clearing member; (c) Credit rating agency; (d) Custodian; (e) Debenture Trustee; (f) Depository participant; (g) Distributor; (h) ESG Ratings and Data Products Provider; (i) Investment adviser; (j) Investment banker; and (k) Research Entity. [Provided that a unit in IFSC desirous of undertaking multiple activities may obtain a unified registration for such multiple activities, in such manner as may be specified by the Authority.]
payload.meaning: Reg 4(1) is the master gate. It names the eleven registrable activities and, since the 2026 amendment, lets a multi-activity unit consolidate them into one unified registration instead of eleven separate certificates.
payload.importance: This is the first thing a Compliance Officer must get right. Operating an unlisted-but-performed activity without the matching certificate is unauthorised activity — a Reg 41 cancellation risk from day one.
payload.takeaway: Eleven named activities; each needs a certificate; multi-activity units may now hold ONE unified registration.
payload.practitioner_note: Inspectors will ask you to reconcile what the unit actually does against what its certificate permits. Keep an activity map. The classic slip is a desk quietly adding an activity (say, distribution) that the original certificate never covered. 'Unified' does not mean 'anything goes' — it means one certificate spanning the activities you actually applied for.

lessons.title: Grant of registration & the 30-day cure

payload.reg_text: (2) If the Authority is of the opinion that the registration cannot be granted, it shall communicate the deficiencies to the Applicant giving it thirty days' time to rectify them. (3) If the Applicant fails to rectify such deficiencies to the satisfaction of the Authority within the specified time, the Authority may refuse to grant registration and shall communicate the same to the Applicant, giving reasons for such refusal: Provided that no such refusal shall be made by the Authority without giving the Applicant an opportunity to make written submissions on the grounds on which the registration is proposed to be refused.
payload.meaning: On being satisfied and on receipt of registration fees, the Authority grants registration subject to conditions. If it cannot grant, it must first flag the deficiencies and give thirty days to fix them; refusal is only permissible after a written-submissions opportunity.
payload.importance: This is the applicant's due-process shield. A registration is never refused out of the blue — there is a mandatory cure window and a right to be heard in writing.
payload.takeaway: Deficiency → 30 days to cure → refusal only after a written-submissions opportunity.
payload.practitioner_note: Do not confuse this thirty-day clock (Reg 12(2), the applicant's cure window) with the thirty-day clock in Reg 5(2) (the exchange/CC/depository forwarding its recommendation). They are different clocks for different parties. When you receive a deficiency letter, treat the 30 days as hard and respond in full — partial cures 'to the satisfaction of the Authority' is the operative test.

lessons.title: Net worth: the number inspectors check first

payload.hook: Net worth is the CMI's licence to keep operating. It is not a one-time entry figure — it must hold at all times. And the CMI framework has three quirks that trip up practitioners from a SEBI or RBI background: a liquid-assets definition for three categories, a highest-not-sum rule for multi-desk units, and no deposit at all.

cards.title: A continuing test, not an entry gate
cards.law: Reg 7(1): an entity shall comply with the net worth requirements in Schedule I, which shall be maintained at all times.
cards.means: Meeting the minimum on application day is not enough; you must stay above it continuously and be able to evidence it.
cards.watch: A quarterly statement of net worth is a mandatory record (Reg 16(1)(d)) — inspectors reconcile it against Schedule I.
cards.link: Ties to Module 5 record-keeping.

cards.title: Three categories measure differently
cards.law: Proviso to Reg 3(1)(cc): for a broker dealer, clearing member or investment banker, 'net worth' means the aggregate value of liquid assets (cash, bank balance, fixed deposits, Government Securities and other specified instruments).
cards.means: These three cannot count illiquid balance-sheet items toward net worth — only liquid assets qualify.
cards.watch: Everyone else uses the ordinary balance-sheet definition. Applying the wrong definition is a common, material error.
cards.link: A signature 'common-or-entity' trap.

cards.title: Multi-category units
cards.law: Reg 7(4): where an entity operates in multiple categories, it shall maintain the highest of the applicable minimum net worth requirements, unless otherwise specified.
cards.means: A unit doing three activities holds the single highest minimum among them — not the sum, not an average.
cards.watch: Do not add the category minimums together; and it is separate from and additional to net worth required for other (non-CMI) activities (Reg 7(3)).
cards.link: Directly tested in the capstone.

payload.summary: Schedule I sets each category's minimum; Reg 7(1) makes it a continuous 'at all times' test; three categories (broker dealer, clearing member, investment banker) measure net worth as liquid assets only (Reg 3(1)(cc) proviso); a multi-category unit holds the highest applicable minimum, not the sum (Reg 7(4)); and there is no deposit requirement anywhere.
payload.tip: Maintain a live net-worth monitor, not a quarter-end scramble. For any unit with a broker-dealer, clearing-member or investment-banker desk, run a parallel liquid-assets computation — the balance-sheet figure can look healthy while the liquid-assets figure breaches.

lessons.title: Net worth requirements

payload.reg_text: (1) An entity seeking registration as a capital market intermediary shall comply with the net worth requirements as specified in Schedule I of these regulations, which shall be maintained at all times. (2) Where a capital market intermediary is set up in the form of branch, the minimum net worth requirements may be maintained at the parent level in the home jurisdiction: Provided that the minimum net worth maintained at the parent level shall be earmarked for its branch in IFSC. (3) The minimum net worth requirements shall be separate and in addition to the minimum net worth requirements applicable for other activities outside IFSC or within IFSC under any other regulations or framework. (4) Where an entity intends to operate as a capital market intermediary in multiple categories, it shall maintain the highest of the applicable minimum net worth requirements, unless otherwise specified by the Authority.
payload.meaning: Reg 7 is the operating rule around the Schedule I numbers: hold it at all times (7(1)); a branch may earmark it at parent level (7(2)); it is ring-fenced from other-activity net worth (7(3)); and a multi-category unit holds the highest single minimum (7(4)).
payload.importance: This one regulation resolves most net-worth disputes: branch structures, entities straddling IFSC and outside, and multi-desk units all find their answer here.
payload.takeaway: At all times · branch earmarks at parent · separate & additional to other activities · highest-of for multi-category.
payload.practitioner_note: The branch earmarking in 7(2) is where inspections get sharp: 'maintained at parent level' is not enough — it must be earmarked for the IFSC branch, and you must be able to show that earmarking. For 7(4), the trap is arithmetic: units instinctively add the minimums. Show the highest-of computation in your net-worth file explicitly.

lessons.title: Definition of 'net worth' and the liquid-assets carve-out

payload.reg_title: Definition of 'net worth' and the liquid-assets carve-out
payload.reg_text: 'net worth' means the aggregate value of the paid-up share capital (or capital contribution) and all reserves created out of the profits, securities premium account and debit or credit balance of profit and loss account, after deducting the aggregate value of the accumulated losses, deferred expenditure and miscellaneous expenditure not written off, as per the balance sheet... Provided that where an entity is a broker dealer, clearing member or investment banker, the 'net worth' shall mean the aggregate value of its liquid assets: Explanation: Liquid assets... shall mean cash and bank balance, fixed deposits, Government Securities and other instruments as may be specified by the Authority.
payload.meaning: Two definitions live in one clause. The default is the ordinary balance-sheet net worth. But for broker dealers, clearing members and investment bankers, net worth means liquid assets only.
payload.importance: Using the wrong definition can flip a 'compliant' unit into breach. The liquid-assets test is deliberately stricter for the three market-facing, settlement-exposed categories.
payload.takeaway: Balance-sheet net worth for most; liquid-assets-only for broker dealer, clearing member and investment banker.
payload.practitioner_note: Keep two computations for any unit touching those three activities: the statutory balance-sheet net worth and the liquid-assets figure. At inspection, be ready to show that the liquid-assets pool (cash, bank, FDs, G-secs, specified instruments) independently clears the Schedule I minimum.

chapters.title: Fit & Proper, Principal Officer & Compliance Officer

lessons.title: The people tests behind every registration

payload.hook: A CMI is only as registrable as its people. Two engines run here: the fit-and-proper test (applied to the entity and its key persons at all times) and the mandatory appointment of a Principal Officer and a separate Compliance Officer, both based in the IFSC.

cards.title: A continuous character test
cards.law: Reg 8(1): a CMI shall ensure that the entity and its principal officer, directors/designated partners, key managerial personnel and controlling shareholders are fit and proper persons, at all times.
cards.means: Fairness, integrity, honesty and good reputation — tested not just at entry but continuously, across a defined list of persons.
cards.watch: A disqualifying event (conviction for moral turpitude/economic offence, pending charge sheet, wilful defaulter, fugitive economic offender, etc.) can taint registration mid-life.
cards.link: Feeds change-in-control (Module 5) and enforcement (Module 6).

cards.title: Principal Officer AND a separate Compliance Officer
cards.law: Reg 9(1): a CMI shall designate a principal officer and a separate compliance officer based out of IFSC.
cards.means: These are two distinct designated roles — you cannot collapse them into one person — and both must be located in the IFSC.
cards.watch: 'Separate' and 'based out of IFSC' are both hard requirements; a shared or offshore officer is a defect.
cards.link: Qualification rules attach to both.

cards.title: Education or experience gateway
cards.law: Reg 9(2): the PO and CO must meet specified educational qualifications (professional qualification or PG degree/diploma in finance, law, accountancy, management, commerce, economics, capital market, banking, insurance, actuarial science, fintech, science, technology, engineering or mathematics; or a graduate with five years' financial-services experience; CA/CS/CMA membership qualifies).
cards.means: There is a defined qualification-or-experience gateway; a law graduate is expressly eligible to be Compliance Officer.
cards.watch: The 'graduate + experience' route was amended to five years (from ten) w.e.f. 12 Jan 2026.
cards.link: Amendment-tracking (old-vs-new).

payload.summary: Reg 8 makes fit-and-proper a continuous test across the entity and its key persons; Reg 9 requires a Principal Officer and a separate Compliance Officer, both based in the IFSC, meeting a defined qualification-or-experience gateway (graduate-plus-experience route eased to five years in 2026).
payload.tip: Run fit-and-proper as an ongoing register, not an onboarding checkbox — capture directors, KMP and controlling shareholders, and re-test on any triggering event. Diarise PO/CO qualification evidence; at inspection, 'separate' and 'IFSC-based' are the first two boxes checked.

lessons.title: Appointment of Principal Officer and Compliance Officer

payload.reg_title: Appointment of Principal Officer and Compliance Officer
payload.reg_text: A capital market intermediary shall designate a principal officer and a separate compliance officer based out of IFSC.
payload.meaning: Every CMI must designate two distinct officers — a Principal Officer and a separate Compliance Officer — and both must be based out of the IFSC.
payload.importance: This is a structural, always-on requirement. A missing, shared, or offshore officer is a standing non-compliance, independent of anything the desks do.
payload.takeaway: Two separate designated officers — Principal Officer and Compliance Officer — both based in the IFSC.
payload.practitioner_note: Inspectors verify three things fast: that both roles exist, that they are different individuals, and that both are genuinely based in the IFSC (not merely named on paper while operating from the parent). For a multi-desk unit, one Compliance Officer can cover the unit, but the role must be real, resourced and resident.

lessons.title: The conduct spine every CMI shares

payload.hook: Whatever your category, one code binds you: Schedule II Part A. Reg 15 makes it mandatory for every CMI. This is the clearest 'common' layer in the whole regulation — and knowing it cold is what lets you separate shared duties from category-specific ones later.

cards.title: Reg 15 imports the whole code
cards.law: Reg 15: a CMI shall abide by the Code of Conduct as specified in Schedule II.
cards.means: The code is not optional guidance — it is a binding regulatory obligation for every CMI, enforceable like any other provision.
cards.watch: Schedule II has two parts: Part A binds all CMIs; Part B adds category-specific codes. Don't stop at Part A for a specific desk.
cards.link: Part B surfaces in each category playbook.

cards.title: No manipulation, no false market
cards.law: Part A cl. 4-5: a CMI shall not indulge in manipulative, fraudulent or deceptive transactions/schemes or spread rumours to distort the market, nor create a false market singly or in collusion.
cards.means: Core market-integrity duties apply to everyone, not just trading desks.
cards.watch: 'Singly or in collusion' — participation in someone else's manipulation counts.
cards.link: Ties to enforcement grounds in Module 6.

cards.title: Confidentiality, conflicts, no exaggeration
cards.law: Part A cl. 7-9: no exaggerated claims about capability/qualifications; maintain client confidentiality except where law requires disclosure; avoid conflicts of interest, disclose them, and have a mechanism to resolve them.
cards.means: A baseline of honesty, confidentiality and conflict-management every CMI owes its clients.
cards.watch: Confidentiality yields only to a legal disclosure obligation — not to commercial convenience.
cards.link: Contrast with category-specific disclosure duties (e.g., IA Reg 34).

payload.summary: Reg 15 imports Schedule II as a binding code; Part A binds every CMI (integrity, no manipulation, no false market, no exaggerated claims, confidentiality, conflict-management, prompt grievance handling, non-discrimination, prompt disclosure of material changes); Part B then layers category-specific codes on top.
payload.tip: Treat Part A as the unit-wide conduct baseline and Part B as the desk overlay. When mapping obligations, tag each conduct duty 'A' (all CMIs) or 'B' (this category) — that tagging is exactly what the capstone tests.

lessons.title: Code of Conduct — all capital market intermediaries

payload.reg_title: Code of Conduct — all capital market intermediaries
payload.reg_text: 1. A CMI shall make all efforts to protect the interest of investors and render the best possible advice to the clients having regard to the needs of the clients, environment and its own professional skills. 2. A CMI shall in the conduct of its business, observe high standards of integrity and fairness and fulfil its obligations in a prompt, ethical and professional manner. 3. A CMI shall at all times exercise due diligence, ensure proper care and exercise independent professional judgment. 4. A CMI shall not indulge in manipulative, fraudulent or deceptive transactions or schemes or spread rumours with a view to distorting market equilibrium or making personal gains. 5. A CMI shall not create false market either singly or in collusion with other intermediaries or the issuer...
payload.meaning: Part A is the universal conduct code: integrity, fairness, due diligence, no manipulation or false market, confidentiality, conflict-management and prompt, professional dealing with clients and the Authority.
payload.importance: Because it binds every category, Part A is the reference point for deciding whether a given conduct duty is 'common' or 'category-specific'. Most integrity duties are Part A; product-level duties tend to be Part B.
payload.takeaway: Reg 15 + Schedule II Part A = the conduct duties every CMI shares, regardless of category.
payload.practitioner_note: In practice, breaches most often surface under Part A cl. 2 (integrity/fairness), cl. 8 (confidentiality) and cl. 9 (conflicts). Build these into staff training and your conflicts register. When an inspector challenges conduct, they will anchor to Part A first, then ask whether a Part B overlay was also missed.

lessons.title: The always-on obligations between inspections

payload.hook: Registration is the gate; Chapter III is the daily discipline. Records, information duties, grievances, dispute resolution, business continuity, cyber, risk, change-in-control, fees and the annual compliance audit — this is the machinery an inspector expects to find running.

cards.title: Eight years, electronically retrievable
cards.law: Reg 16(1): a CMI shall maintain and preserve specified books, records and documents in electronic retrieval form for a minimum of eight years — including a quarterly statement of net worth and AML/CFT/KYC compliance documentation.
cards.means: A defined record set, kept retrievable for eight years, is mandatory — and it explicitly includes your quarterly net-worth evidence.
cards.watch: 'Electronic retrieval form' and 'eight years' are both hard minimums.
cards.link: Net-worth statement ties back to Module 2.

cards.title: 15 days for officer changes; prior approval for control
cards.law: Reg 17(2): intimate any change in PO, CO or KMP within 15 days. Reg 23: a branch intimates a change in control within 15 days; an IFSC-incorporated CMI needs PRIOR approval of the Authority for a change in control.
cards.means: Different triggers, different clocks — and a branch merely notifies control changes, while an incorporated CMI must seek prior approval.
cards.watch: Confusing 'intimate within 15 days' with 'seek prior approval' is a classic error.
cards.link: A structural common-or-entity nuance (branch vs incorporated).

cards.title: BCP, cyber, risk — and a 30 September audit
cards.law: Reg 20-22: maintain a BCP (annually reviewed), a cyber security/resilience framework, and risk-management/internal controls. Reg 25: an annual compliance audit by a CA/CS/CMA member (or foreign-authorised auditor), furnished to the Authority by 30 September.
cards.means: A resilience stack plus an independent annual compliance audit with a fixed filing date.
cards.watch: The audit report deadline is 30 September of the year — diarise it.
cards.link: Cyber detail sits in the separate CSCRF framework.

payload.summary: Chapter III is the continuous-compliance engine: eight-year electronically-retrievable records (incl. quarterly net worth); 15-day intimation of PO/CO/KMP changes; BCP with annual review; cyber and risk frameworks; change-in-control (branch intimates in 15 days, incorporated CMI needs prior approval); fees; and an annual compliance audit filed by 30 September.
payload.tip: Keep a compliance calendar keyed to these clocks — 15-day intimations, annual BCP review, 30 September audit filing — and a control log for change-in-control that distinguishes branch (notify) from incorporated (pre-approve). Inspectors test the machinery, not intentions.

lessons.title: Change in control

payload.reg_text: (1) Where a CMI is operating in the form of branch in an IFSC, it shall intimate the Authority, and the market infrastructure institution of which it is a member (if applicable), within fifteen days of any direct or indirect change in control of the intermediary. (2) Where a CMI is incorporated in an IFSC, it shall seek prior approval of the Authority, in case of any direct or indirect change in control of the intermediary.
payload.meaning: Change-in-control has two regimes by legal form. A branch intimates the change within fifteen days after the fact. An IFSC-incorporated CMI must obtain prior approval before the change.
payload.importance: Getting this backwards is a serious slip: an incorporated CMI that merely notifies (instead of seeking prior approval) has acted without required approval. The distinction turns entirely on legal form.
payload.takeaway: Branch → intimate within 15 days (after). Incorporated in IFSC → prior approval (before).
payload.practitioner_note: Map every unit's legal form to its control-change pathway now, before any transaction is contemplated. For incorporated CMIs, build the IFSCA prior-approval step into deal timelines — it is a condition precedent, not a post-closing formality. Direct AND indirect changes are covered, so watch upstream shareholding moves.

lessons.title: What happens when the Authority looks — and acts

payload.hook: Registration comes with a standing exposure to inspection and, if things go wrong, enforcement. Chapter V sets who can inspect and how; Chapter VI sets the consequence architecture. Knowing the shape of both turns an inspection from an ambush into a managed process.

cards.title: Suo motu, usually on notice
cards.law: Reg 37: the Authority may, suo motu or on information/complaint, appoint an inspecting authority to inspect a CMI's books, systems and procedures; notice is given, but may be dispensed with for reasons recorded in writing where investors' interest requires.
cards.means: Inspection can be triggered proactively; you will normally get notice, but not always.
cards.watch: Exchanges/CCs/depositories may separately inspect BD/CM/DP under their bye-laws; joint inspections are possible.
cards.link: BD/CM/DP carry a dual-oversight layer.

cards.title: Suspension or cancellation grounds
cards.law: Reg 41: the Authority may suspend or cancel registration (or take other action) for failures such as breaching conditions, contravening the Act/regulations, furnishing false or misleading information, non-cooperation in inspection, or failing to resolve investor complaints.
cards.means: A defined set of grounds can cost you your registration.
cards.watch: 'Furnishing false or misleading information in any material particular' is its own standalone ground — accuracy to the Authority is not optional.
cards.link: Ties back to information duties (Module 5).

cards.title: Relaxation and the power to be heard
cards.law: Reg 41 action follows process; Reg 44 lets the Authority relax strict enforcement on application with a non-refundable fee, processed within 30 days. Reg 47 repealed the 2021 CMI Regulations.
cards.means: There is a relaxation mechanism, and enforcement is bounded by process; the 2025 regime replaced the 2021 one.
cards.watch: Relaxation is discretionary and fee-bearing — not a right.
cards.link: Historical context: 2021 → 2025.

payload.summary: Chapter V empowers inspection (suo motu or on complaint, usually on notice, with a dual layer for BD/CM/DP via their market infrastructure institutions); Chapter VI sets enforcement — suspension/cancellation on defined grounds (Reg 41), a fee-bearing relaxation power processed in 30 days (Reg 44), and the repeal of the 2021 Regulations (Reg 47).
payload.tip: Prepare an inspection-readiness pack mapped to Reg 37's purposes (records, compliance, internal controls, fitness, complaints). Because false/misleading information is a standalone Reg 41 ground, institute a single accountable sign-off for everything filed with the Authority.

lessons.title: Suspension, cancellation or other actions

payload.reg_text: The Authority may take such action as deemed fit, including suspension or cancellation of registration, against a CMI if it: (a) fails to comply with any conditions subject to which a certificate of registration has been granted; (b) contravenes any of the provisions of the Act or any rules, regulations, notifications, circulars, guidelines, directions, instructions issued under the Act or any other relevant statute; (c) fails to furnish any information relating to its activity as directed by the Authority; (d) furnishes to the Authority information which is false or misleading in any material particular; (e) does not submit periodic returns or reports as directed; (f) does not co-operate in any enquiry, inspection or investigation; (g) fails to resolve the complaints of investors or fails to give a satisfactory reply to the Authority; or (h) commits any other act/omission which in the opinion of the Authority warrants such action or which is against the interest of the investors.
payload.meaning: Reg 41 is the enforcement backbone: it lists the grounds on which the Authority may suspend, cancel, or otherwise act against a CMI, ranging from condition breaches to false information to non-cooperation and unresolved complaints.
payload.importance: These grounds convert the day-to-day obligations in Chapters II-IV into consequences. Note that recognised exchanges/CCs/depositories may separately suspend BD/CM/DP under their own bye-laws.
payload.takeaway: A defined ground-list drives suspension/cancellation — including false/misleading information and non-cooperation.
payload.practitioner_note: Two grounds deserve standing controls: (d) false/misleading information — put a single accountable owner on every regulatory filing; and (f) non-cooperation in inspection — brief staff that stonewalling an inspection is itself a cancellation ground, independent of the underlying issue. lessons.title: Broker-dealers & clearing members: exchange-tethered

payload.hook: These two categories are unusual: their net worth is set not by IFSCA but by the market infrastructure institution, and their day-to-day rulebook is the exchange's or clearing corporation's bye-laws. cards.title: Comply with the MII bye-laws
cards.law: Reg 26: a broker dealer complies with the recognised stock exchange's bye-laws/rules/regulations; a clearing member complies with the recognised clearing corporation's.
cards.means: Your primary operating rulebook is the MII's, layered on top of the CMI Regulations.
cards.watch: This is also why BD/CM face a dual-oversight layer at inspection and enforcement.

cards.means: Approved role-crossing does not require a new registration, just the MII's approval.
cards.watch: 'Without a separate certificate' is the key phrase — approval, not re-registration.
cards.link: Contrast with adding a genuinely new activity (needs registration).

payload.summary: Broker-dealer and clearing-member net worth is set by the exchange/clearing corporation (not a fixed Schedule I figure), but measured as liquid assets only; their operating rulebook is the MII's bye-laws (Reg 26); and Reg 5(4)-(5) lets them cross roles or operate across multiple MIIs with approval, without a fresh certificate.
payload.tip: For a broker-dealer or clearing-member desk, maintain the liquid-assets net-worth computation continuously and align internal limits to the MII's specified figure. Track approvals under Reg 5(4)-(5) as evidence that role-crossing is authorised.

lessons.title: Credit rating agencies: the rating lifecycle duties

payload.hook: A CRA's registration comes with a USD 200,000 net worth and a set of duties built around the integrity of the rating itself — from the client agreement, through continuous monitoring, to the tightly controlled circumstances in which a rating may be withdrawn.

cards.title: USD 200,000
cards.law: Schedule I, S.No. 3: Credit Rating Agency net worth is USD 200,000 (ordinary balance-sheet definition).
cards.means: A fixed USD figure, measured on the standard net-worth definition (not liquid assets).
cards.watch: Don't apply the liquid-assets carve-out here — that's only BD/CM/IB.
cards.link: Contrast with Module 7.

cards.title: Written agreement per client
cards.law: Reg 28(1): a CRA shall enter into a written agreement with each client whose securities it proposes to rate, setting out rights, liabilities and fees.
cards.means: Every rating relationship is documented up front, including the fee.
cards.watch: No agreement, no rating — the agreement is the foundation.
cards.link: Ties to conflict-management duties in Part B.

cards.title: Continuous monitoring; constrained withdrawal
cards.law: Reg 28(4)-(5): a CRA shall continuously monitor and periodically review ratings unless withdrawn, and shall generally not withdraw a rating while the rated obligations remain outstanding (subject to specified exceptions).
cards.means: A rating is a living obligation — monitored over its life, not a one-off opinion.
cards.watch: Withdrawal while obligations are outstanding is the exception, not the norm.
cards.link: Enforcement exposure if monitoring lapses.

payload.summary: A CRA holds USD 200,000 net worth (standard definition), documents each rating relationship in a written agreement covering rights/liabilities/fees (Reg 28(1)), and treats a rating as a living obligation — continuously monitored and periodically reviewed, and generally not withdrawn while the rated obligations are outstanding (Reg 28(4)-(5)).
payload.tip: Operationalise the 'living rating' duty: a monitoring calendar per outstanding rating, with periodic reviews logged. Because withdrawal is constrained, document the specific triggering exception whenever a rating is withdrawn.

lessons.title: Continuous monitoring and constrained withdrawal

payload.reg_text: (4) A registered credit rating agency shall continuously monitor the rating of securities or other permitted financial products and carry out periodic reviews of the rating, unless the rating is withdrawn. (5) A registered credit rating agency shall generally not withdraw a rating so long as the obligations under the security/instrument/facility rated by it are outstanding: Provided that a registered credit rating agency may withdraw a rating in the following situations...
payload.meaning: A rating is not a point-in-time opinion — the CRA must continuously monitor and periodically review it, and must generally keep it live while the rated obligations are outstanding, withdrawing only in specified situations.
payload.importance: This duty is where CRA inspections bite: a stale or unreviewed rating on a live instrument is a direct contravention, and improper withdrawal removes market information investors rely on.
payload.takeaway: Monitor continuously, review periodically, and don't withdraw a rating while the rated obligations are outstanding (save specified exceptions).
payload.practitioner_note: Keep an auditable monitoring trail for every outstanding rating and a documented rationale mapped to the permitted exceptions for any withdrawal. Inspectors will sample live ratings and ask for the last review date and the monitoring evidence.

payload.summary: A DP's net worth is set by the depository (standard definition), it must open separate accounts per beneficial owner and never commingle holdings (Reg 31(2)), maintain data-processing integrity (31(4)), and reconcile its records with the depository on a daily basis (31(5)).

lessons.title: Investment advisers: fiduciary, fee-only, conflict-clean

payload.hook: The investment adviser holds USD 25,000 net worth, but its defining features are duties, not capital: a fiduciary standard, a prohibition on third-party remuneration, and a 15-day restriction on trading against its own advice.

cards.title: Act in the client's interest, disclose conflicts
cards.law: Reg 34(3): an investment adviser shall act in a fiduciary capacity towards its clients and disclose all conflicts of interest as and when they arise.
cards.means: The adviser is legally bound to put the client first and surface conflicts continuously.
cards.watch: Fiduciary is a higher bar than mere fair dealing.
cards.link: Contrast with distributor's suitability duties.

cards.title: No consideration from anyone but the client
cards.law: Reg 34(4): an IA shall not receive remuneration or compensation in any form from any person other than the client being advised, in respect of the underlying products.
cards.means: No product commissions or third-party payments — the adviser is paid only by the advised client.
cards.watch: This is the sharpest line between an adviser and a distributor.
cards.link: Distributor can be product-remunerated; adviser cannot.

cards.title: 15-day own-account restriction
cards.law: Reg 34(6): an IA shall not transact on its own account contrary to advice given to clients for 15 days from the advice (with a 24-hour-notice exception if its assessment genuinely changes).
cards.means: The adviser cannot trade against its own live advice within the window.
cards.watch: The exception requires a revised assessment communicated to the client at least 24 hours in advance.
cards.link: A precise, testable rule.

payload.summary: An investment adviser (USD 25,000) acts in a fiduciary capacity and discloses conflicts (Reg 34(3)); may be paid only by the client advised, never by third parties (Reg 34(4)); maintains arm's-length between advisory and other activities (34(5)); and must not trade on its own account contrary to its advice for 15 days, save a 24-hour-notice exception (34(6)).

lessons.title: Fee-only advice and the 15-day own-account restriction

payload.reg_title: Fee-only advice and the 15-day own-account restriction
payload.reg_text: (4) An investment adviser shall not receive any consideration by way of remuneration or compensation or in any other form from any person other than the client being advised, in respect of the underlying products or securities for which advice is provided. (6) An investment adviser shall not enter into transactions on its own account which is contrary to the advice given to its clients for a period of 15 days from the day of such advice: Provided that... if the investment adviser is of the opinion that the situation has changed, then it may enter into such a transaction on its own account after giving such revised assessment to the client at least 24 hours in advance...
payload.meaning: Two rules define adviser integrity: the adviser is paid only by the client (no third-party or product remuneration), and it cannot trade against its own advice for 15 days, unless it genuinely reassesses and tells the client at least 24 hours ahead.
payload.importance: Reg 34(4) is what makes an adviser an adviser rather than a distributor. Reg 34(6) prevents the adviser from profiting by trading against the very advice its clients are acting on.
payload.takeaway: Paid only by the advised client; no own-account trading contrary to advice for 15 days (24-hour-notice exception).
payload.practitioner_note: Draw the remuneration line brightly: any trail or commission from a product provider collapses the advisory posture. lessons.title: The four numbers that gate every AIF scheme

payload.hook: Before strategy, before category, four numbers decide whether a scheme can exist at all: corpus, ticket size, investor count and the form units take. Get one wrong and the scheme is defective from launch.

cards.title: Twenty crore a scheme
cards.law: Each scheme of the Alternative Investment Fund shall have corpus of at least twenty crore rupees; each scheme of a social impact fund shall have a corpus of at least five crore rupees.
cards.means: The floor attaches to each SCHEME, not to the fund as a whole. A fund running three schemes must clear it three times.
cards.watch: The five-crore concession is confined to social impact funds. It is not a small-fund exemption.
cards.link: Pairs with the ticket-size rule below.

cards.title: One crore, with two carve-outs
cards.law: The AIF shall not accept from an investor an investment of value less than one crore rupees. Provided that for employees or directors of the AIF or of the Manager, the minimum shall be twenty five lakh rupees. Provided further that this clause shall not apply to an accredited investor.
cards.means: One crore is the general floor; twenty-five lakh for insiders; and the floor does not apply at all to an accredited investor.
cards.watch: The accredited-investor carve-out disapplies the clause entirely — it is not a reduced figure.
cards.link: Accreditation recurs across the regime.

cards.title: One thousand per scheme
cards.law: No scheme of the Alternative Investment Fund shall have more than one thousand investors.
cards.means: A per-scheme ceiling, counted scheme by scheme.
cards.watch: Where the AIF is formed as a company, the Companies Act, 2013 applies in addition.

payload.hook: Category is not just a label for your strategy. It decides whether your fund can be open-ended at all, and how long it may run.

cards.title: Close-ended by category
cards.law: Category I and Category II Alternative Investment Funds shall be close ended and the tenure of the fund or scheme shall be determined at the time of application. Schemes of Category III Alternative Investment Fund may be open ended or close ended.

cards.law: Category I and II Alternative Investment Funds or schemes launched by such funds shall have a minimum tenure of three years.

payload.hook: The regulation makes the Manager or Sponsor put money alongside the investors — and is precise about how much, and how it may not be provided.

payload.hook: Category III is the only category that may employ leverage — but the permission is conditional, and the conditions are where compliance actually lives.

chapters.title: Categories I, II & III: Taxonomy & Sub-Categories

lessons.title: Three categories, one registration slot

payload.hook: An AIF does not choose a category as a label; it registers in exactly one, and the category fixes what it may invest in, whether it may leverage, and whether it may be open-ended. Put a fund in the wrong slot and every downstream condition is wrong.

cards.title: The 'positive spillover' box
cards.law: Category I funds invest in start-ups, early-stage ventures, social ventures, SMEs, infrastructure or other sectors the Board or Government considers socially or economically desirable, and include venture capital funds, SME Funds, angel funds, social impact funds, infrastructure funds and special situation funds.
cards.means: Category I is defined by where it invests and the incentive rationale behind it — not by strategy sophistication. It is a family of named sub-categories, not a single fund type.
cards.watch: Angel funds are a Category I sub-category (inserted 09-09-2025); special situation funds were added earlier (24-01-2022). Older material that lists only VCF/SME/social/infra is out of date.
cards.link: Sub-category selection drives the investment conditions in Chapter 8.

cards.title: The residual box
cards.law: A Category II AIF is one that does not fall in Category I or III and does not undertake leverage or borrowing other than as permitted in these regulations; private equity funds and debt funds for which no specific incentives are given are included.
cards.means: Category II is a residual definition — you land here by not being I or III. Its hallmark is the absence of a leverage strategy, not any positive investment mandate.
cards.watch: 'Does not undertake leverage or borrowing other than as permitted' — the permitted 30-day operational borrowing does not push a fund out of Category II.
cards.link: The permitted borrowing carve-out is drilled in Chapter 8.

cards.title: The only leverage box
cards.law: A Category III AIF employs diverse or complex trading strategies and may employ leverage, including through investment in listed or unlisted derivatives; hedge funds and funds trading for short-term returns are included, and such funds may be open-ended.
cards.means: Category III is the only category defined by permission to leverage as a strategy. It is also the natural home for open-ended, short-horizon funds.
cards.watch: Leverage as a strategy is a Category III marker. A Category I/II fund that merely borrows short-term for operations has not become Category III.
cards.link: Category III's leverage cap and disclosure were covered in Chapter 4.

payload.summary: One registration slot fixes everything: Category I is the named-sub-category, incentive-driven box (VCF, SME, angel, social impact, infrastructure, special situation); Category II is the residual, no-strategic-leverage box (PE, debt); Category III is the only strategic-leverage box (hedge, short-term, may be open-ended).
payload.tip: When a fund's strategy is ambiguous, decide leverage first: strategic leverage forces Category III; its absence, plus no Category I incentive mandate, lands you in Category II by residual definition. Getting the slot right at registration is cheaper than a material-change filing later.

lessons.title: Who the Board lets through the gate

payload.hook: Registration is not a formality. Before a certificate issues, the constitutive documents, the people, and the plan must each clear a named test. Miss one and the application is not deficient — it is ineligible.

cards.title: The documents must permit the activity
cards.law: The memorandum, trust deed or partnership deed must permit the applicant to carry on AIF activity and must prohibit it from inviting the public to subscribe; a trust deed must be registered under the Registration Act, 1908 and an LLP deed filed under the LLP Act, 2008.
cards.means: The fund's own charter has to authorise the business and forbid a public offer. Private placement is baked in at the constitution, not bolted on later.
cards.watch: 'Prohibited from inviting the public' is an eligibility condition, not merely an operating rule — a permissive deed fails Reg. 4(b).
cards.link: Private placement is why the PPM regime (Chapter 9), not a prospectus, governs.

cards.title: The people are tested by an external yardstick
cards.law: The applicant, Sponsor and Manager must be fit and proper persons based on the criteria in Schedule II of the SEBI (Intermediaries) Regulations, 2008.
cards.means: Fit-and-proper is not judged on an AIF-specific scale; it borrows the Intermediaries Regulations standard, covering integrity, competence, financial soundness and record.
cards.watch: The test attaches to three parties — applicant, Sponsor AND Manager. A clean Manager does not cure a tainted Sponsor.
cards.link: The same persons carry the fiduciary duty in Chapter 11.

cards.title: Certification plus qualification
cards.law: The Manager's key investment team must have at least one key personnel with the relevant certification specified by the Board and at least one with a professional qualification in finance, accountancy, business management, commerce, economics, capital market or banking (or a CFA charter); the same person may satisfy both, and fresh certification must be obtained before the existing one expires.
cards.means: The competence gate is now certification-and-qualification, and one qualified, certified person can satisfy both limbs — but the certification must be kept live.
cards.watch: This replaced the old 'five years' experience' test. Answering from the pre-2020/2023 experience rule is a dated-material error.
cards.link: The shift is tracked in Chapter 14.

cards.title: Describe the fund, or fail Reg. 4(i)
cards.law: The applicant must clearly describe, at registration, the investment objective, targeted investors, proposed corpus, investment style or strategy and proposed tenure of the fund or scheme.
cards.means: A vague application is an ineligible application. The regulator wants the fund's shape stated up front, because category, corpus and tenure all flow from it.
cards.watch: Whether the applicant or any Sponsor/Manager entity was earlier refused registration is itself a listed consideration under Reg. 4(j).
cards.link: The stated corpus meets the minimum-corpus gate from Chapter 1.

payload.summary: Eligibility (Reg. 4) is four gates: a constitution that permits AIF activity and forbids a public invitation (trust registered, LLP filed); applicant, Sponsor and Manager all fit and proper on the Intermediaries-Regulations yardstick; a key team meeting the certification-plus-qualification test kept continuously live; and a clearly described objective, investors, corpus, strategy and tenure. The certificate, once granted under a specific category, is valid until the AIF is wound up.
payload.tip: Run eligibility as a checklist across three parties, not one. The most common rejection driver is not the numbers — it is a deed that permits a public invitation, or a Sponsor who fails fit-and-proper while the Manager is clean.

lessons.title: The limits that bind every rupee deployed

payload.hook: Category tells you what a fund is; the investment conditions tell you what it may actually do with the money — how much in one company, whether it may borrow, and how idle cash may sit. These are the rules an inspector reconciles against the portfolio.

cards.title: 25% for I and II, 10% for III
cards.law: Category I and Category II AIFs shall invest not more than twenty-five per cent of investable funds in one investee company; Category III AIFs shall invest not more than ten per cent, with large value funds for accredited investors permitted up to twenty per cent.
cards.means: The single-name cap is tighter for Category III (10%) than for I and II (25%), reflecting Category III's trading character; LVFs get a relaxation to 20%.
cards.watch: The number flips by category. Applying 25% to a Category III fund, or 10% to a Category II fund, is the classic concentration error.
cards.link: The LVF relaxations recur across corpus, PPM and concentration.

cards.title: 30 days, 4 times, 10%
cards.law: Category I and Category II AIFs shall not borrow or leverage for making investments, except to meet temporary funding and day-to-day operational requirements for not more than thirty days, on not more than four occasions in a year, and not more than ten per cent of investable funds.
cards.means: The borrowing carve-out is a narrow operational bridge, fenced by three simultaneous limits — duration, frequency and size — every one of which must hold.
cards.watch: All three limits are cumulative. A 35-day bridge, or a fifth occasion, or 11% of investable funds each independently breaches Reg. 16(1)(c)/17(c).
cards.link: Using this bridge as investment leverage is what pushes a fund into Category III territory (Chapter 6).

cards.title: The venture mandate has a floor
cards.law: At least seventy-five per cent of the investable funds of a venture capital fund shall be invested in unlisted equity shares or equity-linked instruments of a venture capital undertaking, or in companies listed or proposed to be listed on an SME exchange, to be achieved by the end of the fund's life cycle.
cards.means: A VCF cannot drift into being a generalist fund — three-quarters of its money is mandated toward genuine venture and SME exposure, tested over the whole life cycle.
cards.watch: The 75% is measured 'by the end of the life cycle', not at every point in time — an early portfolio below 75% is not automatically in breach.
cards.link: This sub-category floor sits on top of the Category I conditions from Chapter 6.

cards.title: Investments in demat, idle cash parked
cards.law: AIFs shall hold their investments in dematerialised form subject to specified conditions; un-invested investable funds and divestment proceeds pending distribution may be parked in liquid mutual funds, bank deposits or high-quality liquid assets such as Treasury bills, TREPS, commercial papers and certificates of deposit.
cards.means: Two housekeeping rules: portfolio holdings go demat (with narrow carve-outs), and idle money must sit in defined liquid instruments, not be deployed off-mandate.
cards.watch: The demat holding rule (inserted 05-01-2024) is separate from the demat issuance of the fund's own units — do not conflate the two.
cards.link: Dematerialisation is developed in Chapter 12.

payload.summary: Investment conditions bind every deployment: single-company concentration is 25% for Category I and II and 10% for Category III (20% for Category III LVFs); operational borrowing is permitted only within all three limits at once — 30 days, 4 occasions a year, 10% of investable funds; a VCF must reach 75% in unlisted/SME-listed venture exposure by end of life cycle; and holdings sit in demat with idle cash confined to defined liquid instruments.
payload.tip: When you audit a portfolio, test the borrowing carve-out on all three axes at once — practitioners breach it on frequency (a fifth draw) far more often than on the headline 30 days. And always confirm which concentration number applies before you measure a position; the category, not the position size, tells you the cap.

chapters.title: Placement Memorandum & the GARUDA Green Channel

lessons.title: How a scheme actually gets to launch

payload.hook: A scheme is not born when the manager decides to raise money; it is born when a compliant placement memorandum is filed and the launch clock is satisfied. The 2026 GARUDA change rewired that clock — the old wait-for-comments model is gone.

cards.title: The disclosure document, defined
cards.law: The placement memorandum shall disclose investment strategy, risk-management tools, key service providers, the terms of reference of the approving committee, conflicts of interest and the procedures to address them, disciplinary history, the terms on which the Manager offers services, affiliations, and the manner of winding up — all that an investor needs to take an informed decision.
cards.means: The PPM is the AIF's prospectus-equivalent for a private-placement world: it is where strategy, conflicts and exit are disclosed once, in a Board-specified template.
cards.watch: Because the fund is barred from public invitation, the PPM — not a public prospectus — is the governing offer document. Conflicts disclosure is a listed mandatory head, not optional colour.
cards.link: The conflicts duty is enforced through Chapter 11.

cards.title: Through a merchant banker, before launch
cards.law: Schemes may be launched subject to filing the placement memorandum with the Board through a merchant banker at least thirty days prior to launch, with fees under the Second Schedule; the first scheme is exempt from scheme fees, and large value funds for accredited investors are exempt from the filing and comment requirements.
cards.means: Routine schemes route the PPM through a merchant banker who has done independent diligence; the first scheme pays no scheme fee; LVFs skip the filing-and-comment machinery altogether.
cards.watch: Scheme-fee exemption is only for the first scheme — not every scheme. LVF exemption is from the filing/comment step, not from having a PPM.
cards.link: The LVF light-touch runs through corpus, tenure and PPM alike.

cards.title: Rollout upon acknowledgement
cards.law: Under the GARUDA green channel (Green-Channel: AIF Rollout Upon Document Acknowledgement, effective 30 July 2026), an AIF may proceed to launch its regular scheme after ten working days of filing the placement memorandum through a merchant banker who has independently exercised due diligence of the disclosures.
cards.means: GARUDA replaces waiting for SEBI's prior comments with a merchant-banker-diligenced, acknowledgement-based launch after a short working-day window. Speed shifts to the market, accountability shifts to the merchant banker and Manager.
cards.watch: GARUDA is a Master Circular mechanism dated 30-07-2026 — cite it as a circular, never as a regulation. The Manager and merchant banker, not SEBI's silence, carry responsibility for accuracy.
cards.link: Tracked as a 2026 change in Chapter 14.

cards.title: 12 months, and the tenure clock
cards.law: The first close of a scheme shall be declared not later than twelve months from the date the AIF becomes eligible to launch it; the corpus at first close shall not be below the minimum for the category; and the tenure of a close-ended scheme is calculated from the date of first close. If first close is not declared in time, a fresh application and fee are required.
cards.means: First close is the anchor date — it must land within twelve months, must clear the minimum corpus, and it starts the tenure clock. Miss it and you re-file.
cards.watch: Tenure runs from FIRST close, not final close (except legacy schemes that had declared first close by 17-11-2022). Miss the twelve-month window and the scheme must be re-applied for.
cards.link: Tenure and extension were covered in Chapter 2; this is where the clock starts.

payload.summary: A scheme reaches launch through the PPM regime: a Board-template placement memorandum disclosing strategy, conflicts and exit, filed through a merchant banker at least thirty days before launch (first scheme fee-exempt; LVFs exempt from filing/comment). Under GARUDA (30-07-2026) launch follows ten working days after a merchant-banker-diligenced filing rather than awaiting SEBI comments. First close must be declared within twelve months, at or above minimum corpus, and starts the close-ended tenure clock.
payload.tip: Diary the first-close date the moment a scheme is filed — it is the single date that both proves timely launch and starts tenure. Under GARUDA the merchant banker's independent diligence is now the control that used to be SEBI's comment letter; keep that diligence file, because responsibility for PPM accuracy sits with the Manager and merchant banker.

lessons.title: Who may invest, and how they come in

payload.hook: The category rules govern where a fund invests; the onboarding rules govern who may be let in and on what terms. Accreditation is the master key here — it unlocks lighter tickets, co-investment and the LVF regime — so its thresholds must be exact.

cards.title: Two crore, or seven-and-a-half, or the split test
cards.law: An individual, HUF, family trust or sole proprietorship is an accredited investor with annual income of at least two crore rupees; or net worth of at least seven crore fifty lakh rupees of which at least three crore seventy-five lakh is financial assets; or annual income of at least one crore plus net worth of at least five crore of which at least two crore fifty lakh is financial assets.
cards.means: Three alternative routes to individual accreditation — a pure income route, a pure net-worth route, and a combined route with a lower income if net worth backs it up.
cards.watch: The value of the primary residence is excluded from net worth. The three limbs are alternatives — meeting any one qualifies.
cards.link: Accreditation drives the ticket carve-out in Chapter 1 and the LVF regime throughout.

cards.title: Fifty crore for the institutions
cards.law: Trusts other than family trusts, and body corporates, qualify as accredited investors with net worth of at least fifty crore rupees; partnership firms qualify where each partner independently meets the criteria.
cards.means: For institutional forms the single test is a fifty-crore net worth; a partnership must clear it partner-by-partner rather than in aggregate.
cards.watch: Do not carry the individual figures across to entities — the trust/body-corporate threshold is a flat fifty crore, not the seven-and-a-half-crore individual number.
cards.link: Contrast the per-partner test with pooled aggregation.

cards.title: Come direct, pay no distribution fee
cards.law: Schemes of AIFs shall offer investors a Direct Plan, which shall not carry any distribution or placement fee, and investors who approach the AIF directly without a distributor shall be onboarded through the Direct Plan only.
cards.means: An investor who arrives without an intermediary must not be charged distribution economics — the Direct Plan strips the placement fee out entirely.
cards.watch: Direct-arriving investors 'shall' go into the Direct Plan — it is mandatory, not a marketing option, and distribution commission moves to a trail model.
cards.link: Fee governance connects to the obligations in Chapter 11.

cards.title: A ring-fenced side-car for accredited investors
cards.law: Category I and Category II AIFs may offer co-investment to accredited investors through a separate CIV scheme, which must maintain a separate bank and demat account, be ring-fenced from other schemes, and must not borrow or leverage; alternatively co-investment may be facilitated through the portfolio-management route.
cards.means: Co-investment lets accredited investors put extra money alongside the fund into a chosen deal, housed in a ring-fenced CIV scheme with its own accounts and a no-leverage rule.
cards.watch: CIV co-investment is confined to Category I and II AIFs and to accredited investors, and the CIV scheme itself cannot leverage. A Category III fund cannot run a CIV co-investment scheme.
cards.link: Ring-fencing and pari-passu rights recur in Chapter 12.

payload.summary: Onboarding turns on accreditation: an individual qualifies on income of two crore, or net worth of seven crore fifty lakh (three crore seventy-five lakh financial), or one crore income plus five crore net worth (two crore fifty lakh financial), with primary residence excluded; trusts and body corporates qualify at fifty-crore net worth, partnerships partner-by-partner. Every scheme must offer a fee-free Direct Plan, mandatory for investors who arrive without a distributor. Category I and II AIFs may offer accredited investors ring-fenced, non-leveraged CIV co-investment schemes.
payload.tip: Keep the accreditation matrix on one page and check the correct limb — the combined route (one-crore income plus five-crore net worth) is the one advisers most often misquote as a standalone income test. When onboarding a direct-arriving investor, confirm they land in the Direct Plan; charging them a placement fee is a straightforward breach.

chapters.title: General Obligations, Transparency & the Investment Committee

lessons.title: The standing duties between the raise and the exit

payload.hook: Once money is in, the fund runs on standing duties: a fiduciary standard, conflict management, transparency, and periodic reporting. And a governance twist — the people who sit on the investment committee carry the Manager's liability with them.

cards.title: Sponsor and Manager owe the investors
cards.law: The Sponsor and Manager of an AIF shall act in a fiduciary capacity towards the fund's investors, shall disclose all conflicts of interest as and when they arise, and shall monitor and appropriately mitigate conflicts of interest throughout the scope of business.
cards.means: The relationship is fiduciary, not merely contractual — the Sponsor and Manager must put investors first, surface conflicts as they arise, and actively manage them, not just disclose once.
cards.watch: The duty is continuous ('as and when they arise', 'throughout the scope of business') — a one-time PPM disclosure does not discharge it.
cards.link: The conflicts first disclosed in the PPM (Chapter 9) must be managed here.

cards.title: Disclosure is a standing obligation
cards.law: All AIFs shall ensure transparency and disclosure of information to investors, including on financial and material information, fees and charges, and any inquiry or legal action, in the manner specified.
cards.means: Transparency is codified, not cultural: material information, the fee stack and any regulatory action must reach investors as a matter of obligation.
cards.watch: Transparency runs to investors continuously; it is distinct from the periodic reporting the fund owes SEBI.
cards.link: Investor-facing transparency pairs with the SI-Portal reporting below.

cards.title: Sit on the IC, share the liability
cards.law: A Manager may constitute an investment committee to approve investment decisions; the members of such an investment committee shall be equally responsible as the Manager for the fund's investment decisions and for compliance with the regulations.
cards.means: The IC is not an advisory fig leaf. Whoever approves the deals is placed on the same liability footing as the Manager — external members included.
cards.watch: External IC members do not dilute liability; they share it. This is the trap for funds that treat the IC as an outside advisory panel.
cards.link: Liability for default flows through to Chapter 13.

cards.title: SI Portal and the annual CTR
cards.law: AIFs shall file periodic reports on the SEBI Intermediary Portal within the specified calendar-day timelines, and shall submit a Compliance Test Report within thirty days from the end of the financial year, with the trustee or sponsor intimating observations to the manager within thirty days and changes made within fifteen days.
cards.means: Two reporting rhythms: routine activity reporting to the SI Portal on tight day-counts, and an annual compliance self-test (CTR) with a defined review-and-cure loop.
cards.watch: The CTR is annual, from the end of the financial year, with a 30-day file / 30-day intimate / 15-day cure cycle — distinct from the SI-Portal periodic filings.
cards.link: Reporting discipline is what an inspection (Chapter 13) tests first.

payload.summary: The operating phase runs on standing duties: a fiduciary standard on Sponsor and Manager with continuous conflict disclosure and mitigation; codified transparency to investors on material information and fees; an investment committee whose members bear liability equally with the Manager; and periodic reporting to the SEBI Intermediary Portal plus an annual Compliance Test Report on a 30-day file, 30-day intimate, 15-day cure cycle.
payload.tip: Treat the investment committee's liability as the sharpest governance point: if external members approve deals, paper their role, their diligence and their access to information, because the regulator places them on the Manager's liability footing. And run the CTR as a genuine annual self-audit — it is the document an inspector reads before anything else.

lessons.title: The plumbing that protects the investor

payload.hook: Behind the strategy sits the investor-protection plumbing: units held in demat, portfolios valued by an arms-length independent valuer, and every investor holding pari-passu unless they have specifically stepped out. It is unglamorous — and it is exactly what an inspection reconciles.

cards.title: Units and holdings, in demat
cards.law: AIFs shall issue their units in dematerialised form, and schemes above the specified corpus threshold (corpus greater than five hundred crore rupees as on the reference date) were brought into mandatory demat crediting on a phased timeline; investors' units are credited to their demat accounts.
cards.means: Dematerialisation runs on two levels — the fund issues units in demat, and larger funds were phased into mandatory demat crediting first by a corpus threshold.
cards.watch: The five-hundred-crore corpus threshold sequenced the roll-out; it is not a permanent exemption for smaller funds, which follow on the later timeline.
cards.link: Demat holding of the portfolio was flagged in Chapter 8.

cards.title: Arms-length, qualified, tested
cards.law: An AIF shall value its investments through an independent valuer who is not an associate of the manager, sponsor or trustee, who has at least three years' experience in valuation, and who is registered with the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India as a valuer or is a holding company or subsidiary of a credit rating agency; valuation follows the endorsed IPEV guidelines.
cards.means: Valuation independence is defined structurally — no associate relationship — and by qualification: three years' experience plus an IBBI registration or CRA-group status, applying the IPEV standard.
cards.watch: 'Not an associate of the manager, sponsor or trustee' is the core independence test; an in-house or affiliated valuer fails it however qualified.
cards.link: The Manager's non-delegable responsibility for valuation was covered in Chapter 5.

cards.title: 20% flags a material change
cards.law: Where there is a deviation of more than twenty per cent between two consecutive valuations of an asset, or a change in the valuation methodology or approach, the manager shall report it to investors with the reasons, as specified.
cards.means: A large valuation swing or a methodology change is treated as material and must be surfaced to investors — it cannot be smoothed over silently.
cards.watch: The 20% trigger is asset-level and between consecutive valuations; a methodology change triggers reporting independently of the percentage.
cards.link: Materiality and disclosure connect back to Chapter 11 transparency.

cards.title: Equal rights, with named exceptions
cards.law: Investors shall have rights pro-rata to their commitment in each investment and pari-passu in all respects; the pro-rata requirement does not apply where an investor is excused or excluded from a particular investment or has defaulted on a capital call, and differential rights may be offered only without affecting others' pari-passu and pro-rata rights (carried interest excepted).
cards.means: The default is equality — pro-rata by commitment, pari-passu in rights — broken only in named, principled cases: excuse/exclusion, default, or carried interest.
cards.watch: Differential rights are not freely negotiable; they are permitted only where they do not erode other investors' pari-passu and pro-rata position. Excuse/exclusion and default are the recognised pro-rata exceptions.
cards.link: Ring-fencing and equal rights also govern the CIV schemes of Chapter 10.

payload.summary: The investor-protection layer: units issued in demat, with larger funds (corpus above five hundred crore) phased into mandatory demat crediting first; portfolios valued by an independent valuer who is not an associate of manager/sponsor/trustee, has three years' experience and IBBI registration or CRA-group status, applying IPEV; deviations above twenty per cent between consecutive valuations or any methodology change reported to investors; and investors holding pro-rata to commitment and pari-passu, with excuse/exclusion, default and carried interest as the only recognised departures.
payload.tip: When you review a valuation policy, test independence before competence — an affiliated valuer fails the associate test no matter how qualified. And read every side letter against the pari-passu rule: differential rights survive only where they do not erode another investor's pro-rata and pari-passu position.

lessons.title: How a fund is examined, and how it ends

payload.hook: Supervision and exit are the bookend of the lifecycle. SEBI can look in without warning; a fund that fails the rules is dealt with under the Intermediaries machinery; and when a fund's life runs out, there is a defined path through liquidation, dissolution and — new in 2026 — 'Inoperative Fund' status.

cards.title: Suo motu, and notice can be waived
cards.law: The Board may, suo motu or on information or complaint, appoint an Inspecting Authority to examine an AIF's books, records and documents; it shall ordinarily give not less than ten days' notice, but may, where satisfied it is in investors' interest, order inspection without notice.
cards.means: Inspection needs no wrongdoing to begin, and while ten days' notice is the norm, the regulator can dispense with notice entirely where investors' interest demands it.
cards.watch: 'Not less than ten days' notice' is the default, not a guarantee — the no-notice override under Reg. 31(2) is a live power.
cards.link: The cooperation duty makes the inspection workable; see below.

cards.title: Everyone connected must assist
cards.law: Every officer of the AIF and any associated person in possession of relevant information, including the manager, must produce books, accounts and documents, furnish information and extend all cooperation to the Inspecting Authority, which may examine persons on oath and take authenticated copies.
cards.means: The duty to assist reaches beyond the compliance desk to every officer and associated person — and the Inspecting Authority can put them on oath.
cards.watch: The obligation is not confined to the compliance officer; withholding by any connected person is itself a default.
cards.link: Non-cooperation is a listed default trigger below.

cards.title: Dealt with under the Intermediaries route
cards.law: An AIF that contravenes the Act or regulations, furnishes false or misleading information, fails to submit returns, does not cooperate in an inspection, or fails to resolve investor complaints shall be dealt with under the SEBI (Intermediaries) Regulations, 2008, without prejudice to the Board's directions under Reg. 34 or its powers under sections 11, 11B, 11D and related provisions.
cards.means: Enforcement is not free-standing — it is channelled through the Intermediaries Regulations, layered on top of the Board's direction and Section-11 powers.
cards.watch: Non-cooperation in an inspection and failure to resolve investor complaints are themselves default triggers, not merely procedural lapses.
cards.link: Post-inspection, Reg. 34 lets the Board bar new schemes, freeze assets or order refunds.

cards.title: Retention capped, and a 2026 status
cards.law: A trust-form AIF is wound up on expiry of tenure, on a resolution of at least seventy-five per cent of investors by value, or where the Board so directs; unliquidated investments may be distributed in-specie or taken into a dissolution period with seventy-five per cent investor approval; retention of proceeds beyond permissible fund life shall not exceed three years, and a fund may apply to SEBI for 'Inoperative Fund' status (Master Circular, 2026).
cards.means: Exit has structure: a 75%-by-value investor vote or tenure expiry or a Board direction ends the fund; leftovers go in-specie or into a dissolution period; and proceeds can be held only up to three years beyond fund life, after which 'Inoperative Fund' status is the parking bay.
cards.watch: The winding-up and dissolution-period investor thresholds are seventy-five per cent by value; the three-year retention cap and 'Inoperative Fund' status are 2026 circular additions — cite them as circular, not regulation.
cards.link: The 2026 additions are tracked in Chapter 14.

payload.summary: Supervision and exit: SEBI may inspect suo motu with ten days' notice as the norm but a no-notice override in investors' interest, and every officer and associated person must cooperate, on oath if required; a defaulting AIF is dealt with under the SEBI (Intermediaries) Regulations, 2008, with non-cooperation and unresolved complaints as named triggers, and post-inspection directions under Reg. 34; winding up follows tenure expiry, a seventy-five-per-cent-by-value vote or a Board direction, with unliquidated assets going in-specie or into a dissolution period (seventy-five per cent approval), retention capped at three years beyond fund life, and 'Inoperative Fund' status available under the 2026 circular.
payload.tip: Build a standing inspection file — books, CTRs, valuation policy, investor registers — because the ten-day notice can be waived, and the cooperation duty binds every officer, not just compliance. On exit, hold the two seventy-five-per-cent-by-value thresholds and the three-year retention cap precisely; they are the numbers a winding-up plan is judged against.

lessons.title: What changed, when, and from which source

payload.hook: Mastery of the AIF regime is partly a mastery of dates. The last three years reshaped categories, borrowing, dematerialisation and exit — and the two most recent moves, GARUDA and the Inoperative Fund, live in the circular, not the regulation. Knowing which is which is the whole game.

cards.title: The operational carve-out and demat holdings
cards.law: The Fourth Amendment, 2024 (w.e.f. 07-08-2024) recast the Category I and II borrowing carve-out to cover temporary funding and day-to-day operational requirements within 30 days / 4 occasions / 10%; and the requirement to hold investments in dematerialised form was inserted (w.e.f. 05-01-2024).
cards.means: 2024 tightened and clarified the borrowing bridge and pushed the portfolio itself into demat — two operational changes with real audit consequences.
cards.watch: The 2024 borrowing change is to the carve-out wording; it did not create a new leverage freedom. Demat holding of the portfolio is distinct from demat issuance of units.
cards.link: Both are drilled in Chapter 8.

cards.title: A new Category I sub-category
cards.law: The Second Amendment, 2025 (w.e.f. 09-09-2025) brought angel funds expressly within the list of Category I sub-categories in Reg. 3(4), moving them from the earlier standalone Chapter III-A treatment.
cards.means: Angel funds were formally folded into the Category I family — older material treating them as a separate chapter-based construct is out of date.
cards.watch: Angel funds are now a Category I sub-category; listing Category I without them is a dated answer.
cards.link: The current sub-category list is in Chapter 6.

cards.title: The green-channel launch mechanism
cards.law: The GARUDA circular (Green-Channel: AIF Rollout Upon Document Acknowledgement), dated 30 July 2026, allows a regular scheme to launch after ten working days of a merchant-banker-diligenced PPM filing, replacing the wait-for-prior-comments model.
cards.means: GARUDA is the 2026 speed-up of scheme launch, with accountability resting on the merchant banker's independent diligence and the Manager.
cards.watch: GARUDA is a Master Circular mechanism (30-07-2026) — never cite it as a regulation. It changes the launch clock, not the PPM's contents.
cards.link: The launch mechanism is in Chapter 9.

cards.title: Retention capped, a new parking status
cards.law: The June 2026 winding-up circular caps retention of proceeds at three years beyond permissible fund life and introduces 'Inoperative Fund' status, for which an AIF applies to SEBI; the dissolution-period and in-specie routes for unliquidated investments carry a seventy-five-per-cent-by-value investor threshold.
cards.means: 2026 gave the end-of-life a clean architecture: a three-year retention ceiling and an 'Inoperative Fund' parking status, sitting alongside the dissolution-period mechanics.
cards.watch: Retention cap and 'Inoperative Fund' status are circular, dated 2026 — cite them as circular provisions. The exit vote is seventy-five per cent by value.
cards.link: The exit mechanics are in Chapter 13.

payload.summary: The recent reshaping, by date and source: 2024 recast the Category I/II operational borrowing carve-out (07-08-2024) and required demat holding of investments (05-01-2024); 2025 folded angel funds into the Category I sub-categories (09-09-2025); and 2026 delivered two circular-level changes — GARUDA green-channel launch (30-07-2026) and the winding-up circular's three-year retention cap plus 'Inoperative Fund' status. Regulation changes are cited to the amendment regulations; GARUDA and Inoperative Fund are cited to the Master Circular.
payload.tip: Keep a living amendment register with three columns — the change, its effective date, and whether it is regulation or circular. In an inspection or an opinion, the fastest way to lose credibility is to attribute a 2026 circular mechanism like GARUDA or 'Inoperative Fund' to the Regulations; the source label is part of the answer.
